name: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLA) — Technical Summary & Modern Practice
observations: Source: 'RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control', Brohan et al., Google DeepMind, 2023 (arXiv:2307.15818v1, 26 pages, 6k real-world evaluation trials).

Core thesis: a large VLM pretrained on web data can be turned directly into an end-to-end robot policy by co-fine-tuning it on robot trajectories plus the original web vision-language tasks, with NO new parameters and no separate action head. This class of model is named Vision-Language-Action (VLA).

Key idea — 'actions as another language': 6-DoF end-effector delta position (3) + delta rotation (3) + gripper extension + a discrete 'terminate' command = 8 dimensions. Every continuous dimension is discretized into 256 uniform bins, so one action becomes a short string of integers, e.g. '1 128 91 241 5 101 127'.

Action tokenization: reserve 256 existing vocabulary slots as action tokens. PaLI-X already gives integers <=1000 a unique token, so bins map directly to those; PaLM-E has no such mapping, so the 256 least-frequently-used tokens are overwritten (a form of symbol tuning).

Training data format is plain VQA: input = camera image + 'Q: what action should the robot take to [instruction]? A:', output = the action token string. This is what lets language tokens and action tokens share one output space.

Critical recipe detail — CO-fine-tuning beats naive fine-tuning: keep the original web vision-language data (VQA, captioning, interleaved image-text) in the training mixture instead of training on robot data only. This prevents catastrophic forgetting of visual/semantic concepts and is the main driver of generalization. Robot data is upweighted in each batch to balance the mixture.

Decoding constraint: when prompted with a robot-action task, the output vocabulary is restricted to only valid action tokens so the policy can never emit an unexecutable string; on standard vision-language prompts the full natural-language vocabulary is allowed.
Model family: RT-2-PaLI-X built on PaLI-X at 5B and 55B parameters; RT-2-PaLM-E built on PaLM-E at 12B. A smaller PaLI-3B variant was used for the Language-Table simulation benchmark.

Deployment/real-time inference: models are too big for on-robot GPUs, so they are served from a multi-TPU cloud service and queried over the network. The 55B model runs at 1-3 Hz, the 5B model at ~5 Hz, and one service can drive multiple robots.

Robot setup: 7-DoF mobile manipulator, trained on the RT-1 demonstration dataset (13 robots, 17 months, office kitchen environment), each trajectory annotated with a natural-language instruction (verb + object nouns).

Results: on seen tasks RT-2 is roughly on par with RT-1. On unseen objects/backgrounds/environments it gives ~2x improvement over the next-best baselines (RT-1, MOO) and ~6x over the remaining baselines. On emergent-capability benchmarks (symbol understanding, reasoning, human recognition) the best model exceeds RT-1 by >3x average success. Language-Table simulation: RT-2-PaLI-3B 90 +/- 10 vs LAVA 77, RT-1 74, BC-Zero 72.

Emergent capabilities come from semantic/visual transfer only: following instructions never seen in robot data (e.g. 'move apple to 3', 'push coke can on top of heart'), relational reasoning ('move the apple to the cup with the same color'), simple math, multilingual commands ('mueve la manzana al vaso verde'), and person recognition ('move the coke can to the person with glasses').

Chain-of-thought variant: augmented data with an explicit plan, i.e. 'Instruction: I'm hungry. Plan: pick rxbar chocolate. Action: 1 128 124 136 121 158 111 255'. Only a few hundred gradient steps of PaLM-E fine-tuning were needed; this enables multi-stage semantic reasoning (pick a rock as an improvised hammer, pick an energy drink for a tired person) and is an early demo of combining high-level planning and low-level control in one VLA.

Ablations: (1) training a large model from scratch performs very poorly even at 5B; (2) co-fine-tuning generalizes better than robot-data-only fine-tuning at either size; (3) larger parameter count gives better generalization.

Stated limitations: web pretraining adds NO new motor skills — physical competence stays bounded by the robot data distribution; high compute cost makes real-time inference a bottleneck (the paper explicitly calls for quantization and distillation); and very few VLM backbones were publicly fine-tunable at the time.

Practical takeaway for building similar systems today: VLM initialization + co-training on web and robot data + text-tokenized actions + a network-served policy server is the reusable recipe; every main design decision has a modern counterpart in open-source tooling.

name: LeRobot (Hugging Face) — VLA toolkit
observations: Context7 library ID /huggingface/lerobot, version v0.6.1, ~4543 code snippets, high source reputation. End-to-end open-source stack for robot learning: datasets, policies, training, evaluation, Hub sharing.

Canonical workflow mirrors RT-2's data->train->deploy loop as three CLI stages: lerobot-record (collect teleoperated demonstrations into a LeRobotDataset, video-backed v3 format, auto-push to the HF Hub), lerobot-train (train or fine-tune a policy), lerobot-eval (roll out a checkpoint in simulation or on hardware).

SmolVLA is the built-in VLA policy: 'lerobot-train --policy.type=smolvla --policy.load_vlm_weights=true --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/libero ...'. Loading pretrained VLM weights is the direct analogue of RT-2 starting from PaLI-X/PaLM-E rather than from scratch.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is a first-class path: --peft.method_type=LORA --peft.r=64 --peft.lora_alpha=64 with ~10x higher LR (1e-3). This is the practical answer to RT-2's compute-cost limitation.

Prebuilt environments for reproducible evaluation: LIBERO, LIBERO-plus, VLABench, and NVIDIA IsaacLab Arena (e.g. lerobot-eval --policy.path=nvidia/smolvla-arena-gr1-microwave --env.type=isaaclab_arena).

Dataset/robot abstraction is configuration-driven: robot.type=so101_follower, teleop.type=so101_leader, cameras given as an inline dict of opencv devices with explicit width/height/fps; features are derived via hw_to_dataset_features(robot.action_features, 'action').

Policies and datasets are distributed through the Hugging Face Hub by repo_id, so a trained policy is one path string away from being evaluated elsewhere — the open-source equivalent of RT-2's centralized served checkpoint.

name: OpenPI (Physical Intelligence) — pi0 / pi0.5 VLA models
observations: Context7 library ID /physical-intelligence/openpi, ~203 code snippets, high source reputation. Open weights and packages for flow-based vision-language-action models.
Base checkpoints pretrained on 10k+ hours of robot data and intended for fine-tuning: pi0_base, pi0_fast_base (autoregressive variant), pi05_base at gs://openpi-assets/checkpoints/*.

Architectural contrast with RT-2: pi0 uses flow matching for continuous action generation rather than RT-2's discretized text-token action bins — evidence that discrete tokenization was a 2023-era choice, not a requirement.

Serving pattern is the direct descendant of RT-2's cloud inference: 'uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=[DROID|ALOHA|LIBERO]' starts a policy server (default port 8000) that the robot control loop queries remotely, decoupling a large model from the robot's onboard compute.
Fine-tuning on custom data: 'uv run scripts/train.py pi05_droid_finetune --exp-name=my_experiment --overwrite', with the dataset/checkpoint swap done entirely in config.py.
Both JAX and PyTorch checkpoints are supported; the same serve_policy.py command works with a converted PyTorch checkpoint directory.
